Write both energies in terms of the displacement and substitute **x = A/2**.
**Step 1 — write the two energies.**
PE = ½kx² ✓
KE = total − PE = ½kA² − ½kx² = **½k(A² − x²)** ✓
**Step 2 — substitute x = A/2.**
PE = ½k(A²/4) = **kA²/8**
KE = ½k(A² − A²/4) = ½k(3A²/4) = **3kA²/8** ✓
**Step 3 — take the ratio.**
KE : PE = 3 : 1 ✓
**The general formula.**
KE/PE = (A² − x²)/x² ✓
At x = A/2 this is (1 − ¼)/¼ = **3**, as found.
**The energy picture across a cycle.**
at the **mean position**, x = 0: all **kinetic**, ratio **infinite** ✓
at **x = A/2**: KE is **75%** of the total, PE **25%** ✓
at **x = A/√2**: the two are **equal** ✓
at the **extremes**, x = A: all **potential**, ratio **zero** ✓
**Why the energies are not equal at half amplitude.** Both depend on the **square** of
a displacement ✓ Half the amplitude means only a **quarter** of the potential energy -
which is why the particle still has three quarters of its energy as kinetic.
**Where the two are equal.** Setting A² − x² = x² gives
x = A/√2 = **0·707A** ✓ considerably further out than half amplitude.
**The total energy, for reference.**
E = ½kA² = **½mω²A²** ✓ constant throughout the motion, independent of where the
particle happens to be.
**A worked instance.** With k = 100 N m⁻¹ and A = 0·1 m:
E = ½(100)(0·01) = **0·5 J**
at x = 0·05 m: PE = ½(100)(0·0025) = **0·125 J**, KE = **0·375 J** ✓
ratio **3 : 1** ✓
**How the energies vary in time.** Both oscillate at **twice** the frequency of the
motion ✓ since they go as sin²ωt and cos²ωt. Their sum stays constant, which is simply
sin² + cos² = 1.
**Reading the distractors.** **1 : 3** ✗ inverts the ratio. **4 : 1** ✗ and **8 : 1** ✗
correspond to x = A/√5 and x = A/3 ✓ Substituting into (A² − x²)/x² checks any of them
in one line.
∴ 3 : 1.

Amplitude modulation produces the carrier **plus two sidebands**.
**Step 1 — write the modulated signal.** With a carrier of frequency ω_c and a message
of frequency ω_m,
y = A_c(1 + µ cos ω_m t) cos ω_c t ✓
**Step 2 — expand the product.** Using the identity for a product of cosines,
y = A_c cos ω_c t
+ (µA_c/2) cos(ω_c + ω_m)t
+ (µA_c/2) cos(ω_c − ω_m)t ✓
**Step 3 — read off the three components.**
the **carrier** at ω_c
the **upper sideband** at ω_c + ω_m ✓
the **lower sideband** at ω_c − ω_m ✓
So an AM wave contains **one carrier with two side-band frequencies** ✓
**A worked instance.** A 1000 kHz carrier modulated by a 5 kHz audio tone:
carrier: **1000 kHz**
upper sideband: **1005 kHz**
lower sideband: **995 kHz** ✓
and the signal occupies **10 kHz** of the spectrum.
**The bandwidth rule.**
**bandwidth = 2 x (highest modulating frequency)** ✓
which is why medium-wave broadcast stations are spaced 9 or 10 kHz apart - closer
spacing would let the sidebands overlap and stations interfere.
**Where the information lies.** Entirely in the **sidebands** ✓ The carrier conveys no
information at all - it is simply a reference. That realisation led to
**single-sideband** transmission, which suppresses the carrier and one sideband and
sends the same message in half the bandwidth with a fraction of the power.
**How the power divides.** For 100% modulation, the carrier takes **two thirds** of the
total power and the two sidebands one sixth each ✓ so AM is inherently inefficient - the
price of a receiver simple enough to be built from a diode and a coil.
**Why modulation is needed at all.** Audio frequencies would need antennas kilometres
long and would all interfere with one another ✓ Shifting the message up to a high
carrier frequency makes practical antennas possible and lets many stations share the
spectrum.
**Reading the distractors.** "**One carrier**" alone ✗ would carry no information.
"**Infinite frequencies**" ✗ would need a non-sinusoidal message. "**One carrier with
high frequency**" ✗ describes the carrier but omits the sidebands ✓
∴ one carrier with two side band frequencies.

Maximum kinetic energy is the **total** energy, ½mω²A².
**Step 1 — read the amplitude and angular frequency.** From
x = 6·0 cos(100t + π/4) cm:
A = 6·0 cm = **0·06 m** ✓
ω = **100 rad s⁻¹** ✓
**Step 2 — apply the formula.**
KE_max = ½mω²A²
= ½(1)(100)²(0·06)² ✓
**Step 3 — evaluate.**
(100)² = **10⁴**
(0·06)² = **3·6 x 10⁻³**
KE_max = ½(10⁴)(3·6 x 10⁻³)
= ½(36)
= **18 J** ✓
**Why the maximum KE equals the total energy.** At the **mean position** the
displacement is zero, so the potential energy is zero and all the energy is kinetic ✓
E = KE_max = **18 J**, and that total is constant throughout the motion.
**The maximum speed.**
v_max = ωA = 100 x 0·06 = **6 m s⁻¹** ✓
and ½mv² = ½(1)(36) = **18 J** ✓ confirming the answer by a second route.
**Why the units matter so much.** The amplitude is given in **centimetres** ✓ Using 6
instead of 0·06 would give 180 kJ - four orders of magnitude out. Converting at the
start is essential.
**What the phase constant π/4 does.** It fixes **where the particle was at t = 0**, and
nothing else ✓ It has no effect on the amplitude, the frequency or the energy, and is in
the question only to see whether that is understood.
**The other quantities.**
period: T = 2π/100 = **0·0628 s**
frequency: **15·9 Hz**
force constant: k = mω² = **10⁴ N m⁻¹** ✓ a stiff spring, which is why the energy is
substantial for so small an amplitude.
**The maximum acceleration.**
a_max = ω²A = 10⁴ x 0·06 = **600 m s⁻²** ✓ about 61g - a violent oscillation.
**Reading the distractors.** **9 J** ✗ omits the factor of ½ somewhere, or halves the
answer; **6 J** ✗ and **3 J** ✗ are smaller still ✓ Checking against ½mv²_max with
v_max = ωA = 6 m s⁻¹ settles it immediately.
∴ 18 J.

A **silvered lens** acts as a mirror whose power is **2P_lens + P_mirror**.
**Step 1 — write the power of the combination.** Light passes through the lens, reflects
and passes through again:
**P = 2P_L + P_M** ✓
**Step 2 — note that the silvered surface is plane.** A plane mirror has **infinite**
focal length, so
**P_M = 0** ✓
**Step 3 — relate the effective focal length to the lens.**
P = 2P_L, so
1/F = 2/f_L
**f_L = 2F** = 2(0·2) = **0·4 m** ✓
(taking magnitudes, since the combination behaves as a concave mirror of focal length
0·2 m).
**Step 4 — apply the lens-maker's formula.** For a plano-convex lens, one surface is
flat:
1/f_L = (n − 1)(1/R)
so
R = (n − 1)f_L
= (1·5 − 1)(0·4)
= **0·2 m** ✓
**Why the light passes through the lens twice.** Once on the way in and once after
reflection ✓ which is why the lens's power is counted **twice** in the combination - the
single most important point in these problems.
**The companion case.** Silvering the **curved** surface instead would give
P_M = 2/R = 2/0·2 = 10 D, and
P = 2(2·5) + 10 = **15 D**, F = **6·7 cm** ✓ a much more powerful mirror. Which surface
is silvered changes the answer completely.
**Why the combination is converging.** Both the converging lens and - in the curved
case - the concave mirror add positive power ✓ With a plane back surface the lens alone
does all the work, twice over.
**A check on the numbers.**
f_L = R/(n − 1) = 0·2/0·5 = **0·4 m** ✓
F = f_L/2 = **0·2 m** ✓ exactly as given.
**The general formula.** For a lens of focal length f silvered on one side with a mirror
of focal length f_m,
1/F = 2/f + 1/f_m ✓
**Reading the distractors.** **0·4 m** ✗ is the **lens's** focal length, not its radius
of curvature - the commonest slip, since it appears in the working. **0·1 m** ✗ and
**0·75 m** ✗ match no step ✓
∴ 0.2 m.

With the film on one side gone, the **surface tension of the remaining film** pulls the
thread taut away from the punctured region.
**Step 1 — see the situation before puncturing.** Film covers **both** sides of the
thread, A and B ✓ Each pulls with the same surface tension, so the forces balance and
the loose thread keeps whatever irregular shape it happens to have.
**Step 2 — puncture A.** The film in A is destroyed, so its pull **vanishes** ✓ Only
the film in B still pulls.
**Step 3 — see what B's film does.** A film always tries to **minimise its area** ✓ so
it contracts, dragging the thread **towards B** - that is, **away from A**.
**Step 4 — describe the resulting shape.** Bulging away from A means the thread becomes
**convex towards A** ✓ and it is pulled into a smooth **circular arc**, since a circle
encloses the greatest area for a given perimeter - which is what minimises the film's
remaining area.
**Why an arc of a circle.** The film pulls with equal force per unit length everywhere
along the thread ✓ The only shape in which a uniform inward pull is balanced at every
point by the thread's tension is a **circular** arc.
**The classic demonstration.** A loose loop of thread floating on a soap film takes no
particular shape; puncture the film **inside** the loop and it snaps instantly into a
perfect **circle** ✓ a beautiful and memorable experiment.
**Why surface tension exists.** Molecules at a surface have fewer neighbours than those
in the bulk, so the surface carries extra energy ✓ The film reduces that energy by
reducing its area - which appears to us as a tension pulling the boundary inward.
**Why a soap film has two surfaces.** Front and back ✓ so the force on a length l of
thread is **2Sl**, not Sl - a factor that matters when calculating, though not for the
direction here.
**Why the relative sizes of A and B do not matter.** The pull per unit length is the
same for any soap film, whatever its area ✓ so the thread always moves away from the
punctured side. That disposes of the "depends on the size" option.
**Reading the distractors.** "**Concave towards A**" ✗ has the thread bulging **into**
the punctured region, as though the vanished film were still pulling. "**Remains in the
initial position**" ✗ would need the forces still balanced ✓
∴ becomes convex towards A.

Dispersive power is the **difference** in refractive index between the extremes, divided
by the **mean** index minus one.
**Step 1 — state the definition.**
ω = (n_V − n_R)/(n_Y − 1) ✓
with n_Y the index for the mean - yellow - colour.
**Step 2 — substitute.**
ω = (1·67 − 1·63)/(1·65 − 1)
= 0·04/0·65 ✓
**Step 3 — evaluate.**
= **0·0615** ✓
**Why the denominator is n − 1 and not n.** The **deviation** produced by a thin prism
is
δ = (n − 1)A ✓
so it is n − 1, not n, that measures a material's refracting power. Dispersive power is
the ratio of the **spread** of deviations to the **mean** deviation:
ω = (δ_V − δ_R)/δ_Y = (n_V − n_R)/(n_Y − 1) ✓
**What the number means.** ω = 0·0615 says the spread between violet and red is about
**6%** of the mean deviation ✓ Flint glass, with ω around 0·05, disperses more strongly
than crown glass at about 0·02 - which is why flint is used for prisms and crown for
achromatic lenses.
**Why ω is dimensionless.** It is a ratio of two refractive-index differences ✓ so it
is a pure number characterising the **material**, independent of the prism's angle or
size.
**A worked consequence.** For a 10° prism of this material:
δ_Y = (0·65)(10) = **6·5°**
angular dispersion = (1·67 − 1·63)(10) = **0·4°** ✓
and 0·4/6·5 = **0·0615** ✓ confirming the definition.
**Why an achromatic combination is possible.** Two prisms of different materials can be
arranged so their **dispersions** cancel while a net **deviation** survives ✓ The
condition is ω₁δ₁ = ω₂δ₂, which is why the two glasses must have different ω.
**The one caveat.** ω varies slightly with which pair of wavelengths is chosen as the
extremes ✓ Optical designers use standardised Fraunhofer lines - F, d and C - and quote
the reciprocal, the **Abbe number**, instead.
**Reading the distractors.** **0·024** ✗ divides by 1·65 instead of 0·65 - the
commonest error. **1·60** ✗ is 0·04/0·025, inverting something, and **0·031** ✗ halves
the correct value ✓
∴ 0.0615.

A rainbow needs **dispersion** to separate the colours and **total internal reflection**
to send them back towards the observer.
**Step 1 — follow a ray into a raindrop.** Sunlight **refracts** on entering the
spherical drop, and because the refractive index differs slightly with wavelength, the
colours are **dispersed** ✓
**Step 2 — follow it inside.** The ray strikes the back of the drop at an angle beyond
the critical angle for water, so it is **totally internally reflected** ✓
**Step 3 — follow it out.** It refracts again on leaving, **further separating** the
colours ✓
**Step 4 — conclude.** Both **dispersion and total internal reflection** are needed ✓
**The geometry of the primary bow.** Red emerges at about **42°** from the antisolar
direction and violet at about **40°** ✓ so red is on the **outside** of the arc. The
bow is seen only when the Sun is **behind** the observer, and it is always a circle
centred on the shadow of one's head.
**Why it is an arc at all.** Every drop at exactly 42° from the antisolar point sends
red light to the eye ✓ Those drops form a **cone**, whose intersection with the sheet of
rain is the circular arc we see.
**The secondary bow.** A fainter arc at about **51°**, produced by **two** internal
reflections ✓ The extra reflection reverses the order, so red is on the **inside** - and
the extra loss at each reflection is why it is dimmer. Between the two lies
**Alexander's dark band**, where no light emerges.
**Why refraction alone is not enough.** Refraction separates the colours, but without
the internal reflection the light would pass straight through the drop and continue
**away** from the observer ✓ It is the reflection that turns it back.
**Why total internal reflection alone is not enough.** That would send white light back
unchanged, with no colours ✓ Dispersion is what makes a rainbow coloured rather than a
bright white arc.
**Why not scattering.** Scattering explains the **blue sky** and red sunsets, not the
rainbow ✓ Rainbow light comes from drops large compared with the wavelength, where
geometrical optics applies.
**Why rainbows are polarised.** The internal reflection occurs near Brewster's angle,
so the light is about **96% polarised** ✓ Rotate a polarising filter and a rainbow can
be made to disappear - a striking confirmation of the mechanism.
∴ dispersion and total internal reflection.

Two thin lenses of **equal but opposite** focal lengths in contact have **zero** net
power.
**Step 1 — write the combination formula.** For thin lenses in contact,
1/F = 1/f₁ + 1/f₂ ✓
**Step 2 — substitute.** The convex lens has +f and the concave one the **same**
magnitude, so −f:
1/F = 1/f + 1/(−f)
= **0** ✓
**Step 3 — interpret.**
**F = ∞** ✓
The combination has no converging or diverging power at all: parallel rays emerge
**still parallel**, and the focus moves to **infinity**.
**Why the powers simply add.** Power is P = 1/f, and for thin lenses in contact
P = P₁ + P₂ ✓
Here +P and −P, so the total is zero. A zero-power combination is optically equivalent
to a **flat plate of glass**.
**A worked instance.** A +20 cm convex lens with a −20 cm concave lens:
P₁ = **+5 D**, P₂ = **−5 D**, total **0 D** ✓
**What such a combination is good for.** Nothing by itself - but the same idea with
**different** glasses makes an **achromatic doublet** ✓ There the powers do not quite
cancel; the **dispersions** do, leaving a net converging power free of colour fringing.
Every decent camera and telescope objective is built this way.
**The physical picture.** The convex lens starts bending the rays towards the axis, and
the concave lens immediately bends them back by exactly the same amount ✓ The rays leave
in the direction they arrived.
**A caution about "in contact".** The simple addition of powers holds only for **thin**
lenses touching ✓ Separate them by a distance d and
1/F = 1/f₁ + 1/f₂ − d/(f₁f₂)
which is **not** zero - and that is the basis of the Galilean telescope and the
beam expander.
**Why the question says "of the same focal length".** It guarantees exact cancellation ✓
A slightly weaker concave lens would leave a residual converging power and a finite,
longer focal length - which is the first distractor's "shifts away by a small distance".
**Reading the distractors.** "**Focus undisturbed**" ✗ would need the second lens to
have no power. "**Shifts away by a small distance**" ✗ is the unequal-focal-length case ✓
∴ the focus shifts to infinity.

To send out a **parallel beam**, the source must sit at the **focus** of a **concave**
mirror.
**Step 1 — use the reversibility of light.** A concave mirror brings a parallel beam to
its focus ✓ Reverse the rays: a source **at** the focus sends out a **parallel** beam.
**Step 2 — check the other mirrors.**
**plane mirror** ✗ - reflects a diverging beam as a diverging beam, with the image as
far behind as the object is in front. It cannot collimate anything.
**convex mirror** ✗ - makes a diverging beam **more** divergent, since its focus is
virtual. It spreads light out, which is why it is used for wide-angle viewing.
**Step 3 — conclude.** Only the **concave** mirror produces a parallel beam ✓
**Where this is used.** Searchlights, car headlamps, torches and solar cookers all put
the source - or the target - at the focus of a concave reflector ✓ Reflecting
telescopes use the same geometry in reverse, collecting parallel starlight at the focus.
**Why a paraboloid, not a sphere, in practice.** A spherical mirror suffers **spherical
aberration**: rays far from the axis cross the axis nearer the mirror ✓ A **parabolic**
reflector focuses **all** parallel rays to a single point exactly, which is why car
headlamps and satellite dishes are parabolic.
**The mirror formula, as a check.**
1/v + 1/u = 1/f ✓
with the object at the focus, u = −f:
1/v = 1/f − 1/f = 0, so **v = ∞** ✓ the reflected rays meet only at infinity - that is,
they are parallel.
**How precise the placement must be.** Very ✓ A source even slightly off the focus sends
out a slowly converging or diverging beam, which is why headlamp bulbs are mounted to
tight tolerances and why a torch's beam can be focused by sliding the reflector.
**What happens if the source is not a point.** A real filament has size, so the beam
always has some spread ✓ The smaller the source relative to the mirror, the better the
collimation - which is why laser pointers, with an almost point-like source, produce
such tight beams.
**The lens equivalent.** A **convex lens** with the source at its focus does the same
job ✓ but mirrors are preferred for large apertures: no chromatic aberration, and they
can be supported from behind.
∴ Concave mirror.
